name: Chicken Teriyaki Donburi
instructions: Mix soy sauce, mirin, sugar, and ginger for sauce.
Pan-fry chicken until browned on both sides.
Pour sauce over chicken, simmer until thick and glossy.
Slice chicken into strips.
Serve over steamed rice with sauce drizzled on top.
tips: Use chicken thighs for juicier results — breast meat dries out faster.

name: Katsu Curry
instructions: Bread and deep-fry the cutlets until golden, then slice.
Sauté onion, carrot, and potato until softened.
Add water and simmer, then dissolve curry roux.
Cook until thick and glossy.
Serve curry over rice, topped with sliced katsu.
tips: Add a spoon of honey or grated apple for a sweeter, restaurant-style curry.

name: Oyako Don (Chicken & Egg Rice Bowl)
instructions: Simmer chicken and onion in dashi-soy-mirin sauce until cooked.
Pour beaten eggs over the chicken.
Cover and cook until eggs are softly set.
Slide everything over a bowl of hot rice.
Garnish with mitsuba or green onions.
tips: The name ‘oyako’ means parent-and-child (chicken and egg) — a classic comfort donburi.

name: Yakisoba (Stir-fried Noodles)
instructions: Stir-fry the meat until almost cooked.
Add vegetables and cook until slightly wilted.
Add noodles and yakisoba sauce, tossing quickly.
Cook until everything is well coated and hot.
Serve topped with aonori, pickled ginger, and mayonnaise.
tips: Street-style yakisoba is often cooked on a large flat teppan — high heat is key.

name: Tonkatsu (Breaded Pork Cutlet)
instructions: Pound pork lightly, season with salt and pepper.
Coat in flour, then egg, then panko.
Deep-fry or pan-fry until golden and cooked through.
Drain on a rack, slice into strips.
Serve with shredded cabbage, tonkatsu sauce, and rice.
tips: Let the breaded cutlets rest a few minutes before frying for better adhesion of the crumbs.

name: Soba Noodle Soup (Kake Soba)
instructions: Cook soba according to package, rinse under cold water.
Heat dashi with soy sauce and mirin to make the broth.
Place noodles in bowls and pour hot broth over.
Top with green onion, nori, and kamaboko.
Serve immediately.
tips: Rinsing the soba removes excess starch and keeps the noodles springy.

name: Kung Pao Chicken
instructions: Marinate chicken in soy sauce and cornstarch for 15 min.
Stir-fry chicken in hot oil until cooked through.
Add dried chilies and peanuts, toss quickly.
Pour in vinegar-soy sauce mixture.
Stir until sauce coats everything. Serve with rice.
tips: Have all ingredients prepped before cooking — this dish moves fast!

name: Dan Dan Noodles

ingredients.name: Chili oil + soy sauce + black vinegar

instructions: Cook noodles until just done, drain and set aside.
Stir-fry ground pork with ya cai until crispy and fragrant.
Mix sauce: chili oil, soy sauce, black vinegar, Sichuan pepper oil.
Place noodles in bowls, top with pork mixture.
Pour sauce over and toss vigorously before eating.
tips: The key is the fragrant, numbing Sichuan peppercorn oil — don’t skip it.

name: Mapo Tofu
instructions: Stir-fry ground pork until browned.
Add doubanjiang, garlic, and ginger, cook until fragrant.
Pour in a little stock or water and bring to a simmer.
Gently add tofu and simmer 5–7 minutes.
Finish with ground Sichuan pepper and green onions. Serve with rice.
tips: The classic version is very numbing and spicy — adjust Sichuan pepper to your tolerance.

name: Beef Chow Fun (Dry-Fried Rice Noodles)

ingredients.name: Dark soy sauce + light soy sauce

instructions: Marinate beef with soy sauce and cornstarch.
Stir-fry beef quickly over very high heat, remove.
Stir-fry noodles with dark soy for color.
Add bean sprouts, green onion, and beef back in.
Toss everything rapidly and serve immediately.
tips: This dish needs extremely high heat (wok hei) — a screaming hot wok is essential.

name: Tomato Egg Noodles
instructions: Cook noodles and set aside.
Scramble eggs, remove from pan.
Stir-fry tomatoes with garlic until saucy, season with sugar and salt.
Return eggs, toss with noodles.
Finish with green onion and serve.
tips: A simple home-style lunch that comes together very quickly.

name: Stir-fried Water Spinach
instructions: Wash and cut water spinach into lengths.
Stir-fry garlic (and belacan/chili if using) until fragrant.
Add the greens and toss on high heat until just wilted.
Season lightly with soy sauce.
Serve immediately as a vegetable side or light lunch with rice.
tips: Cook very quickly on high heat so the stems stay crunchy.

name: Japchae (Stir-fried Glass Noodles)
instructions: Cook glass noodles until soft, rinse and cut into shorter lengths.
Stir-fry each vegetable and the protein separately.
Season noodles with soy sauce, sugar, and sesame oil.
Toss everything together until well combined.
Finish with more sesame oil and sesame seeds.
tips: Don’t overcook the noodles — they should stay springy, not mushy.

name: Sundubu Jjigae (Soft Tofu Stew)
instructions: Sauté garlic, onion, and gochugaru in a little oil.
Add stock and bring to a boil.
Add seafood/pork and vegetables, simmer a few minutes.
Gently add the soft tofu and crack an egg on top.
Serve bubbling hot with rice.
tips: Traditionally served in a ttukbaegi (earthenware pot) that keeps it boiling at the table.

name: Bulgogi (Marinated Beef)
instructions: Mix soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil, grated garlic, and grated pear for marinade.
Marinate beef for at least 20 minutes.
Stir-fry or grill the beef with onion until cooked and caramelized.
Finish with green onion and sesame seeds.
Serve with rice and banchan.
tips: The grated pear tenderizes the meat and adds natural sweetness.

name: Doenjang Jjigae (Soybean Paste Stew)
instructions: Bring stock to a boil and dissolve doenjang.
Add potato, zucchini, onion, and pork if using.
Simmer until vegetables are tender.
Add tofu and green chili, cook a few more minutes.
Garnish with green onion and serve with rice.
tips: A staple everyday Korean stew — deep, earthy, and very comforting.

name: Samgyeopsal (Grilled Pork Belly)
instructions: Grill pork belly slices on a pan or tabletop grill until crispy and cooked.
Cut into bite-sized pieces.
Wrap a piece of pork with ssamjang, garlic, and chili in a lettuce or perilla leaf.
Eat as ssam (wraps) with kimchi on the side.
tips: The classic Korean BBQ experience — best shared and eaten immediately while hot.

name: Jjajangmyeon (Black Bean Noodles)
instructions: Stir-fry chunjang in oil until fragrant and slightly toasted.
Add pork and vegetables, cook until soft.
Add water/stock and simmer into a thick sauce.
Cook noodles, drain, and place in bowls.
Pour the black bean sauce over and top with cucumber.
tips: Toasting the black bean paste removes bitterness and deepens the flavor.

name: Chicken Adobo
instructions: Marinate chicken in soy sauce, vinegar, and garlic for 30 min.
Sauté garlic until golden in a pot.
Add chicken and brown on all sides.
Pour in marinade, add bay leaves and peppercorns.
Simmer 40 minutes until tender. Serve with rice.
tips: Never stir the adobo while the vinegar is boiling — it makes it sour.

name: Pancit Canton
instructions: Soak or briefly boil noodles until just pliable.
Stir-fry meat until cooked, then push aside.
Add vegetables and stir-fry quickly.
Add noodles and sauces, toss until everything is coated.
Serve with calamansi wedges on the side.
tips: Pancit is traditionally served at birthdays for long life — don’t cut the noodles!

name: Sinigang na Baboy (Pork Sinigang)
instructions: Boil pork until tender (about 40 minutes).
Add onion, tomatoes, and radish, cook 10 minutes.
Add tamarind mix and vegetables.
Season with fish sauce.
Serve hot with rice.
tips: The sourness should be bright but balanced — adjust tamarind and fish sauce to your taste.

name: Ginisang Monggo (Mung Bean Stew)
instructions: Boil mung beans until soft and starting to break down.
In another pan, sauté garlic, onion, tomato, and meat.
Combine with the mung beans and simmer.
Add leafy greens at the end.
Season with fish sauce and serve with rice.
tips: A very common everyday Filipino lunch — comforting and budget-friendly.

name: Paksiw na Pata
instructions: Place the pork hock in a pot with soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, bay leaves, and peppercorns.
Add enough water to cover the meat.
Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 1–1.5 hours until the pork is very tender.
Add banana blossoms if using, and a little brown sugar if you like it slightly sweet.
Simmer a few more minutes until the sauce reduces. Serve with rice.
tips: A classic Filipino lunch dish — the long simmer makes the pork fall-off-the-bone tender. Perfect with lots of rice.

name: Dinuguan (Pork Blood Stew)
instructions: Sauté garlic and onion, then brown the pork.
Add vinegar and bay leaf, simmer without stirring until the vinegar cooks off.
Add a little water or stock and cook until pork is tender.
Lower heat and slowly stir in the pork blood until thickened.
Season with fish sauce and add green chili. Serve with rice or puto.
tips: Stir the blood in gradually over low heat so it doesn’t curdle. Best eaten with soft puto or rice.

name: Sisig
instructions: Boil or grill the pork until cooked, then chop finely.
Sauté onion and chili, add the chopped pork.
Season with soy sauce, calamansi, and a bit of mayonnaise or butter if desired.
Serve sizzling on a hot plate, optionally topped with a raw egg.
tips: Classic Kapampangan sisig is chopped and served sizzling — very popular as a lunch or pulutan dish.

name: Bicol Express
instructions: Sauté garlic, onion, and ginger, then add pork and brown.
Add shrimp paste and chilies, cook until fragrant.
Pour in coconut milk and simmer until the pork is tender and the sauce thickens.
Adjust seasoning and chili level.
Serve hot with rice.
tips: A fiery Bicolano dish — the coconut milk balances the heat from the chilies and bagoong.

name: Pad Thai
instructions: Soak rice noodles in warm water for 30 minutes.
Stir-fry tofu and shrimp until cooked.
Add noodles and sauce (tamarind + fish sauce + sugar).
Toss with bean sprouts and garlic chives.
Serve topped with crushed peanuts and lime wedge.
tips: Don't oversoak the noodles — they'll continue cooking in the wok.

name: Tom Yum Goong (Spicy Shrimp Soup)
instructions: Bring water or stock to a boil with lemongrass, galangal, and lime leaves.
Add mushrooms and tomatoes, simmer 5 minutes.
Add shrimp and cook until just pink.
Season with fish sauce, lime juice, and crushed chilies.
Finish with fresh cilantro and serve hot.
tips: Add a splash of evaporated milk or coconut milk if you prefer Tom Yum Nam Khon (creamy version).

name: Khao Pad (Thai Fried Rice)

ingredients.name: Fish sauce + soy sauce + white pepper

instructions: Stir-fry garlic and protein until cooked.
Push aside, scramble the egg.
Add rice and break it up, seasoning with fish sauce and soy sauce.
Add tomato and green onion at the end.
Serve with cucumber slices, lime, and prik nam pla.
tips: Day-old rice is much better — fresh rice becomes mushy.

name: Green Curry (Gaeng Keow Wan)
instructions: Fry the green curry paste in a little coconut cream until fragrant.
Add the remaining coconut milk and bring to a simmer.
Add chicken/tofu and vegetables, cook until done.
Season with fish sauce and palm sugar.
Finish with Thai basil and serve with rice.
tips: Use good-quality green curry paste or make your own for the best flavor.

name: Som Tum (Green Papaya Salad)
instructions: Pound garlic, chili, and dried shrimp in a mortar.
Add long beans and lightly bruise.
Add shredded papaya, tomato, and the dressing (fish sauce, lime, sugar).
Toss and pound lightly to mix.
Top with crushed peanuts and serve with sticky rice or as a side.
tips: The balance of sour, salty, sweet, and spicy is everything — taste and adjust as you pound.

name: Moo Ping (Grilled Pork Skewers)

ingredients.name: Coconut milk + soy sauce + sugar + garlic

instructions: Marinate pork in coconut milk, soy sauce, sugar, and garlic for at least 20 minutes.
Thread onto skewers.
Grill over medium heat until caramelized and cooked through.
Serve with sticky rice and a simple dipping sauce.
tips: A popular Thai street lunch or snack — the slight sweetness from the coconut marinade is key.
